title: First incompleteness: Gödel sentences and Rosser's theorem

based_on.title: An Introduction to Gödel's Theorems, second edition, corrected Logic Matters reprint

summary: Construct arithmetic sentences that a consistent, effectively axiomatized extension of Robinson arithmetic can neither prove nor refute.
abstract: Could enough axioms make arithmetic settle every sentence? If the axioms can be listed by a program, the theory is consistent, and it contains Robinson arithmetic, Rosser’s theorem says no. We construct an undecided sentence by comparing possible proofs of opposite conclusions. Gödel’s original construction makes the underlying idea especially clear: a sentence asserts that it has no proof, and consistency prevents the theory from proving it. Excluding a proof of its negation takes a stronger assumption in that argument. The distinction explains Rosser’s improvement and leads to a further limit: no consistent extension of Robinson arithmetic has a computable test for its theorems.
